subject: chemistry
title: Tests for carbonate, halide and sulfate ions
key_idea: Negative ions are identified with a reagent and a result. Carbonates fizz with dilute acid and the gas turns limewater milky. Halides give a precipitate with silver nitrate, and its colour shows which halide. Sulfates give a white precipitate with barium chloride.

blocks.text: (Separate science) This section covers how to show that a compound contains carbonate ions, CO₃²⁻.

items.meaning: A negative ion, such as carbonate, chloride or sulfate.
A solution of calcium hydroxide, used to test for carbon dioxide.

items.text: Add dilute acid to the sample.
Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas.
Limewater turns milky (cloudy) if the gas is carbon dioxide.

items: Carbonate plus dilute acid gives carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.

blocks.text: This section covers how to tell chloride, bromide and iodide ions apart.

items: Add dilute **nitric acid** to the solution first.
Then add **silver nitrate** solution.
A precipitate forms. Its colour shows which halide ion is present.

blocks.text: Why nitric acid, not hydrochloric acid

items: Hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions.
Chloride ions would give a white precipitate with silver nitrate.
This would interfere with the test, so a different acid is used.
Use dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution.
White is chloride, cream is bromide and yellow is iodide.

blocks.text: This section covers the test for sulfate ions, SO₄²⁻, and how to choose and use the three anion tests.

items: Add dilute **hydrochloric acid** to the solution.
Then add **barium chloride** solution.
A **white precipitate** (barium sulfate) shows that sulfate ions are present.
Sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions.
Using it would give a white precipitate whatever the sample contains.
The result would not show that the sample contains sulfate ions.

blocks.text: Pick an anion to see which reagent to add and what you see.

diagram.alt: Choose an anion to see the reagents used and the result of the test.

options.label: Carbonate
results: Dilute acid, then limewater for the gas

options.label: Chloride
results: Dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate

options.label: Bromide
results: Dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate

options.label: Iodide
results: Dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate

options.label: Sulfate
results: Dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride

items: Sulfate: dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride. A white precipitate forms.
Never use an acid that contains the ion you are testing for.

checks.q: Describe a test for carbonate ions and the result.
checks.a: Add dilute acid. Bubble the gas given off through limewater. The limewater turns milky (cloudy).

checks.q: A solution gives a cream precipitate when dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution are added. Name the ion present.
Explain why dilute hydrochloric acid is used, not dilute sulfuric acid, in the test for sulfate ions.
checks.a: Sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions, so it would give a white precipitate with barium chloride whatever the sample contains.

worked_example.question:
Describe a test to identify the presence of sulfate ions in a solution of potash alum.

Give the result of the test.
answer_points: Add barium chloride solution (barium nitrate solution is allowed).
Add dilute hydrochloric acid (dilute nitric acid is allowed).
A white precipitate forms (this mark depends on the barium chloride being added).
worked_example.tip: One mark for each reagent and one for the result. The result only counts if barium chloride was added.

worked_example.question:
A sample of the potassium chloride was also tested for chloride ions.
Describe the test for chloride ions.
worked_example.tip: Hydrochloric acid and sulfuric acid are rejected for the first mark. The result mark depends on silver nitrate.

worked_example.question:
Chemical tests are used to identify gases, anions and cations.

Leila has an unknown solution.

She thinks that the solution contains copper(II) ions and bromide ions.

Describe the chemical tests she does to confirm the presence of these two ions in the solution.
answer_points: Copper(II) ions: add aqueous sodium hydroxide.
Bromide ions: add dilute nitric acid and aqueous silver nitrate.
worked_example.tip: Each ion needs a reagent mark and a result mark. In the standard halide test, add the dilute nitric acid first, then the silver nitrate. Another soluble metal hydroxide or aqueous ammonia is allowed for the copper test.

worked_example.question:
Solid F is calcium carbonate. A student adds about 15 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid to a sample of solid F in a boiling tube and tests any gas produced.

Describe the observations.

blocks.text: This course asks for three more anion tests, and a different acid for sulfate.

items: **Nitrate, NO₃⁻**: add aqueous sodium hydroxide and aluminium foil, and warm. Ammonia gas is made, and it turns damp red litmus paper blue.
**Sulfate, SO₄²⁻**: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate. A white precipitate forms.
**Sulfite, SO₃²⁻**: add acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII). The purple solution turns colourless.

worked_example.question:
This question is about ionic compounds.

A student has four unlabelled beakers, each containing a colourless solution of a different salt.

These are the four salt solutions.
• calcium bromide
• calcium chloride
• sodium chloride
• sodium sulfate

Describe a series of tests to identify each solution. Do not refer to safety precautions in your answer.
answer_points: Any two from the flame test points: do a flame test (M1); sodium chloride and sodium sulfate give a yellow flame (M2); calcium chloride and calcium bromide give an orange-red flame (M3)

Any four from the anion tests: add acidified silver nitrate, or nitric acid and silver nitrate (M4); calcium bromide gives a cream precipitate (M5); calcium chloride and sodium chloride give a white precipitate (M6); add acidified barium chloride (M7); sodium sulfate gives a white precipitate (M8)
worked_example.tip: Do not use hydrochloric or sulfuric acid to acidify the silver nitrate test.
